Abstract

This study has been pre-registered (https://osf.io/hnbuk/overview?view_only=95735d00b11d484db42d7b2661e6ca14). We thank Morgane Hoffmann for her help in extracting data from information systems, designing the study, and proofreading the first version of the manuscript. We thank members of the LPC who participated in the translation process: Thibaud Kinnig, Anne Hillairet de Boisferon, Florence Spitzenstetter, Marie Riebel, Eva Commissaire, Elena Costache, Camille Sanrey, Thomas Lehoux and Hiba Errajraji. We also thank Sophie Middleton, the professional psychologist who participated in the backtranslation step. We gratefully acknowledge funding from the

French Translation and Validation of the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale

Unemployment has widespread detrimental personal, interpersonal, sociological, and economic consequences (Brand, 2015; Wanberg, 2012). Among its many effects, unemployment negatively affects one's physical (McKee-Ryan et al., 2005) and mental (McKee-Ryan et al., 2005; Paul & Moser, 2009), life satisfaction (Gedikli et al., 2023), selfesteem and self-efficacy (Creed et al., 2001). Conversely, individuals who become reemployed return to their baseline levels of subjective well-being, even when the working conditions are less favorable than those of their previous position (Zhou et al., 2019).

Consequently, much research has been conducted on the determinants of job search behavior and subsequent employment access for unemployed people.

Among these frameworks, self-regulatory frameworks define job search as "a goaldirected, self-regulatory process in which cognition, affect, and behavior are devoted to preparing for, identifying, and pursuing job opportunities" (van Hooft et al., 2021). This job search process unfolds over time in contexts that are highly ambiguous, uncertain, and competitive (Kanfer et al., 2001; van Hooft et al., 2021; Wanberg, 2012). Consequently, individuals need to set goals, break them down into manageable plans, and initiate and sustain job search behavior in the face of multiple setbacks and degraded psychological abilities.

From this perspective, job search self-efficacy (JSSE), "the belief that one can successfully perform specific job search behaviors and obtain employment" (Saks et al., 2015, p. 115), is a central determinant of the job search process.

Job search self-efficacy is a concept of shared interest from multiple perspectives

Theoretically, JSSE is a core component of dominant frameworks explaining the job search process. It is related to perceived behavioral control in the theory of planned job search behavior (Ajzen, 1991; van Hooft, 2018). It is also a key motivational resource in selfregulatory job search models, as it operates at all stages of the job search process, relating to job search goal settings, self-regulation, the intensity and quality of job search behavior, and employment outcomes, including status and quality (van Hooft et al., 2021). Another major theoretical framework integrating job search self-efficacy is the Social Cognitive Career Theory (Lent et al., 1994), which considers JSSE as an important "proximal antecedent" of search goals, search actions and outcomes (Lent & Brown, 2013, p. 565). In this specific theoretical framework, a recent meta-analysis and a recent scoping review insisted on the value of further studying JSSE and its consequences in longitudinal settings to target field interventions accordingly (Kim et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025).

From an applied perspective, JSSE is of interest as it is malleable and can be targeted in job search interventions (Eden & Aviram, 1993). For example, the JOBS program has been shown to increase participants' JSSE, which mediated the program's effects on job search behavior, reemployment, and mental health (Price et al., 1992; Van Ryn & Vinokur, 1992; Vinokur & Schul, 1997). Furthermore, meta-analytic evidence suggests that interventions that boost self-efficacy are more effective at helping unemployed people find employment than interventions that do not target self-efficacy (Liu et al., 2014). Finally, JSSE could be used to identify unemployed people with the lowest self-efficacy, who may need and benefit the most from support (Roques, 2008; van Hooft et al., 2021; Vinokur et al., 1995; Wanberg et al., 2010). Therefore, it is crucial for researchers focusing on the job search process and for organizations implementing programs that support unemployed people to have a reliable tool to measure JSSE.

From interest to the need for a valid measure

As its definition implies, JSSE encompasses two conceptually distinct beliefs, namely the belief that one can successfully perform job search behavior and the belief that one can obtain employment. For three decades, however, the measurement of JSSE has varied considerably from study to study, with no generally accepted scale (Saks et al., 2015). Many studies have conflated these two constructs or mixed them with others by combining items referring to job search knowledge, abilities, behavior, and outcomes into a single composite score. To address this issue, Saks et al. (2015) constructed and validated a two-dimensional measure. In their study, JSSE behavior predicts job search intention and behavior, and JSSE outcome predicts the number of job offers received. Teye-Kwadjo (2021) strengthened their work by validating the scale structure using an item response theory approach. Taken together, these findings suggest a reliable measure of JSSE.

Building on their work, the present study translates and validates a French version of the JSSE scale while addressing four limitations of prior research. First, we draw on a large sample of unemployed people registered with the French public employment service, of which 2,055 were used, whereas prior validations relied on smaller samples or samples of students (Saks et al., 2015; Teye-Kwadjo, 2021; Zheng et al., 2025). Second, we collected objective job search behavior and access to employment from administrative records, rather than self-reported job search behavior or employment outcomes declared by participants (Saks et al., 2015; Teye-Kwadjo, 2021; Zheng et al., 2025). Third, we adopted a longitudinal approach, collecting these outcomes within 90-day (three month) and 150-day (five-month), overcoming the limitations of previous cross-sectional studies (Kim et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025). Fourth, half of the initially sampled unemployed people was randomly assigned not to receive the survey, to rule out a potential measurement effect where measuring self-efficacy altered subsequent job search behavior (Zwane et al., 2011). The method and hypotheses were pre-registered (see the Methods section).

Hypotheses and research questions

Hypotheses and research questions are divided into four categories: (1) structure and reliability of the scale, (2) validity of the scale, (3) predictive validity of the scale and (4) exploratory research questions.

Structure and reliability of the scale

Concerning the structure, we expected the scale to be a two-factor structure with correlated factors of approximately r = .69, as in the original study (H1a; Saks et al., 2015). Its internal consistency should be close to Saks et al.'s (2015) results of α = .89 for JSSE behavior and α = .96 for JSSE outcome (H1b).

To assess scale reliability, we expected to find a positive Pearson correlation between the JSSE subscales at T1 and T2. Since this had not been assessed in previous research, we anticipated the correlation to be above r = .60 (H2).

Validity of the scale

Convergent validity was tested against self-esteem and motivation to (re)work. First, self-esteem is a general evaluation of one's self-worth (Rosenberg, 1965), while JSSE is an evaluation of one's abilities in a specific domain. Therefore, both belong to the broader family of self-evaluation (Kanfer et al., 2001; van Hooft et al., 2021). Accordingly, we expected the scale to positively correlate with Rosenberg's (1965) self-esteem scale (H3), with a correlation equivalent to that observed by Creed et al. (2001, r = .50). Second, according to self-determination theory, perceived competence is a basic psychological need that supports intrinsic motivation (Ryan & Deci, 2000b). Conversely, amotivation arises from not valuing an activity, not feeling competent to perform it, or not expecting it to yield desired outcomes (Ryan & Deci, 2000a). The latter two sources map directly onto low JSSE behavior and low JSSE outcome. Camus et al. (2017) developed a French scale to measure motivation to (re)work among unemployed people. Consistent with this rationale, they found that general self-efficacy was positively correlated with autonomous motivation (r = .35). However, they also found that general self-efficacy was not correlated with amotivation (r = -.21). This null result may be due to insufficient statistical power, given that their sample size was only 54.

Thus, we expected JSSE to correlate positively with autonomous motivation to ( re)work (H4a)and negatively with amotivation to ( re

Predictive validity of the scale

Regarding predictive validity, we expected JSSE to predict job search behavior as well as the outcomes of that search (Kanfer et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2019; Saks et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2025). More precisely, following Saks et al. (2015), we posited that both JSSE behavior

Exploratory research questions

We had three exploratory research questions for which we did not formulate any directional hypotheses.

First, JSSE may be related to the assistance that unemployed people receive from their job counselor, who can forward job openings that match their profile. For example, greater JSSE could motivate individuals to complete their online profiles more thoroughly and share higher-quality resumes. Consequently, unemployed people who display higher self-efficacy may be perceived by their counselor as better suited for available positions and, therefore, be forwarded more job openings. However, these openings still require the unemployed person to apply, reflecting a counselor-initiated opportunity that the unemployed person then acts upon (RQ1). Second, JSSE may be related to job proposals initiated directly by recruiters. A higher level of self-efficacy may result in a more comprehensive and detailed profile on the public employment service's online platform, giving the impression of greater employment readiness, which may attract more direct proposals from recruiters (RQ2). Thus, access to employment can be achieved through three channels, namely applications initiated by the unemployed person (H6), openings forwarded by a counselor (RQ1), and proposals initiated by recruiters (RQ2). Examining these channels together helps us understand the pathways through which JSSE might relate to employment.

Finally, JSSE behavior and outcome may vary according to sociodemographic factors (age, gender, level of education, nationality, family situation, number of children to care for, length of registration with the public employment service, number of unemployment benefits days remaining, administrative category in which the person is registered, type of support from the public employment service; RQ3; Kanfer et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2019).

Methods

The study protocol and hypotheses were preregistered, and any deviations from the preregistration are noted. Anonymized survey responses, research materials, and R scripts are available on OSF (https://osf.io/hnbuk/overview?view_only=95735d00b11d484db42d7b2661e6ca14). Demographics and outcomes, which are proprietary, cannot be shared.

Translating the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale into French

We translated the 20-item scale by Saks et al. (2015) into French using the translate/back-translate method suggested by Chapman and Carter (Chapman & Carter, 1979) and subsequently refined by Cha et al. (Cha et al., 2007).

First, three researchers from the first author's lab, who were proficient in English and not involved in the research, independently translated the original scale into French. This resulted in three French versions of the scale. Second, another group of three researchers from the same lab, who were also not involved in the research and unfamiliar with the original scale, compared these three versions with one another. This working group concluded that only a few minor adjustments were necessary, as the three versions were already very similar. Specifically, they decided to replace some words with synonyms that did not change the core Minor differences were noted, such as variations in figurative language and the use of synonyms 1 . These differences did not affect the meaning, resulting in a good fit between the original version and its French translation.

Since the scale was intended for unemployed people, it was first presented to a group of employment counselors before being sent to unemployed people. This group was not familiar with the research or the original scale, was tasked with determining whether the scale 1 One of the participants in this step had a British background, whereas the original scale was developed in an American context. Some differences between the back-translated version and the original were attributed to this cultural difference.

was understandable to unemployed people, and whether it targeted the most important job search practices. The group validated the 20-item French version of the scale and advocated for the addition of a 21 st item that they felt was missing. This item assessed sending unsolicited job applications, an important job search strategy in the French context (Rémy & Bergeat, 2017). It was formulated as follows: "Send unsolicited applications to get a job interview. 2 " This item was theoretically grouped with the JSSE behavior subscale. This final step resulted in 21 statements that were tested further. The final French scale and the original English one, along with filling instructions, can be found in Appendix 1.

Sample and contact procedure

This study was conducted in collaboration with France's public employment service, France Travail. It provides services to unemployed people, supports employers in their recruitment processes, and facilitates employment policies at the national and regional levels.

Its most popular service is providing unemployment benefits to eligible individuals, which encourages people to register with the organization. A random sample of 60,000 unemployed people was extracted, from a total pool of approximately 5,000,000 registered individuals, in June 2023. Sampled participants were 18 years old or older, were required to be actively looking for a job, had a confirmed email address, and had agreed to receive emails and surveys. To test for a measurement effect, half of the sample was randomly assigned to receive the survey, while the other half was not. The survey sections and item order were randomized. Participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey, which adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Helsinki Protocol for Human Research and ethical standards. Participants were not paid. Participation was clearly stated to be voluntary and anonymous, with no possible consequences for participants or their unemployment benefits.

2 "Faire des candidatures spontanées pour obtenir un entretien d'embauche."

Unemployed people were emailed twice to complete a survey. The first email was sent in early June 2023 (T1), and the second was sent at the end of June to ensure a one-month interval between responses (T2). A reminder email was sent one week after each initial email.

Answers were paired with data from the public employment service's information system using an individual identifier and an anonymizing table. This made it possible to extract job search behavior and access to employment within 90-day (three months) and 150-day (five months), respectively.

Measures

The internal consistency of each scale was assessed by computing hierarchical omega and Cronbach's alpha, along with their bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 10,000 bootstrap confidence intervals (Kelley, 2026).

Job Search Self-Efficacy

The French version of the JSSE scale consists of 21 statements, such as "Prepare a sales pitch that will attract the interest of employers" (JSSE behavior) or "Obtain more than one good job offer" (JSSE outcome). Participants were asked to indicate their level of confidence for each listed behavior or outcome on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident). Internal consistency indices are reported in the Results section.

Self-Esteem

Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by Vallieres and Vallerand (1990). The scale consists of ten items, such as "On the whole, I am satisfied with myself", with which participants indicate their level of agreement on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The scale had good internal consistency (α = .85 [.83; .86]; ω = .84 [.83; .86]).

Motivation to (re)work

Participants answered the Motivation to (Re)work Scale by Camus et al. (2017). The scale consists of five subscales that assess autonomous motivation, identified regulation, external social regulation, external material regulation, and amotivation. Although the entire scale was presented to preserve its coherence, we only had hypotheses about the autonomous motivation and amotivation subscales, as only these two are related to JSSE. The scale contains 17 items, such as "I want to go back to work because I really enjoy it" (autonomous motivation) and "I don't see the point of going back to work" (amotivation). Participants indicated their level of agreement with each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The scale had good internal consistency for the autonomous motivation (α = .85 [.84; .87]; ω = .85 [.84; .87]), the identified regulation (α = .76 [.74; .78]; ω = .76 [.74; .78]), external social regulation (α = .64 [.61; .67]; ω = .70 [.66; .73]), external material regulation (α = .74 [.71; .76]; ω = .75 [.72; .77]), and amotivation (α = .76 [.73; .79]; ω = .76 [.73; .79]) subscales.

Behavioral outcomes

Behavioral outcomes were extracted from the public employment service's information system 90 days (three months) after the initial survey was sent out.

For unemployed people, the behavioral measures were the number of job applications submitted, the number of clicks on job postings on the public employment service platform, and the amount of time spent on the platform.

For job counselors, the behavioral measures were the number of job openings the counselor forwarded to the unemployed person.

For recruiters, the behavioral measures were the number of proposals a recruiter sent to the unemployed person through the platform.

All behavioral outcomes were winsorized at the 99 th percentile (values above that threshold were recoded to that threshold's value).

Job search engagement

Although it was not pre-registered, we created a job search engagement score to complement the single-behavior count outcomes. This score deliberately combined both flow and stock indicators to provide a broader, more sensitive exploratory summary of overall job search engagement. Six binary indicators were aggregated, and one point was assigned for each of the following: sending at least one application within 90 days; clicking on at least one job posting within 90 days; visiting the platform at least once within 90 days; having created an online profile on the public employment service website; having uploaded a résumé to the online platform; and having made this profile publicly accessible to recruiters.

Job search outcomes

Job search outcomes were drawn from objective administrative records 150-day (five months) after the initial survey was sent out, capturing whether the person obtained employment anywhere in the country.

The preregistration identified two types of employment outcomes: precarious employment, which includes temporary agency work and fixed-term contracts shorter than six months, and stable employment, which includes permanent contracts. However, the information system did not record contract duration, so the precarious employment category could not be constructed. Therefore, we report employment at the level of detail available in the administrative records. This decomposition is more detailed than the preregistered dichotomy, and we consider this deviation to increase the informativeness of the employment analyses. Contrary to our expectations, the information as to whether a person created a company was not available among the extracted data. Therefore, we could not include this specific outcome in our analysis.

Job search outcomes included obtaining any job (permanent, fixed term, or temporary agency employment), obtaining any standard employment (permanent or fixed term employment), obtaining a permanent job only, obtaining a fixed term job only, and obtaining a temporary agency job only.

Demographics

Demographics were measured using the public employment service's information system. For categorical variables, the first category is the reference one in regressions: gender

Results

Sample description

A total of 2,226 people completed the survey. This represents approximately 7% of the initial sample of 30,000 people who were randomly assigned to receive the survey. As preregistered, 11 participants were removed because their responses showed a variance below 0.50 across all items, and 160 respondents were removed because their responses showed a 3 Members of all categories were unemployed and required to engage in job search behavior.

variance below 0.50 for at least half of the scales. This suggests that these respondents provided nearly identical responses throughout the survey, despite the inclusion of reverseworded items and constructs. The total sample of 2,055 people at T1 was, on average, 44 years old (SD = 12, min = 18, max = 69) and predominantly female (n = 1,310). A table showing the sociodemographic balance between respondents and non-respondents is provided in Appendix 2. Respondents differed from non-respondents on nearly all observed characteristics, and were older, more educated, and more often of French nationality. The consequences are discussed in the Limitations section.

Comparing the group randomly assigned to receive the survey with the group that was not, receiving the survey had no measurable effect on job search behavior or access to employment (Appendix 3). This absence of a question-behavior effect indicates that measuring self-efficacy did not itself alter subsequent behavior (Zwane et al., 2011).

A sample of 1,159 follow-up responses was received at T2, of which 998 were complete. After applying the same data cleaning procedure, 897 answers were retained. Of the responses, 859 could be merged from respondents at T1 and T2.

Structure and reliability of the scale

Pre-registered fit indices were derived from Hu and Bentler (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) should be below .06, the comparative fit index (CFI) and the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) should both exceed .95, and the standardized root mean residual (SRMR) should be below .06. Because these cutoffs were derived using maximum likelihood estimation under certain conditions, they do not generalize to other models that do not meet these conditions, or to categorical estimators. We therefore complemented them with dynamic fit index cutoffs, which are tailored to the characteristics of the specific model and data through Monte Carlo simulation (McNeish & Wolf, 2023). These last indices were not pre-registered.

Structure of the scale: Exploratory factor analysis

As pre-registered, to test the two-factor structure with correlated factors hypothesis (H1a), an Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) with oblimin rotation and a robust maximum likelihood estimator was conducted on a random subsample of 210 respondents at T1 (Rosseel, 2012).

The one-factor model showed inadequate fit and explained 44.5% of the variance (χ2 = 427(189), p < .001; CFI = .868; TLI = .853; RMSEA = .089 [.077; .100]; SRMR = .068).

The two-factor model showed a good fit (χ2 = 256(169), p < .001; CFI = .954; TLI = .942; RMSEA = .056 [.041; .069]; SRMR = .041) and yielded two correlated latent factors of r = .65 [.55; .76]. It reproduced the JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome distinction, the former latent factor explaining 26.3% of the variance and the latter 24.4%. Extracting a third factor did not meaningfully improve fit (χ2 = 253(150), p < .001; CFI = .956; TLI = .939; RMSEA = .057 [.045; .069]; SRMR = .035) and produced a third factor that explained only 8.4% of the variance. The two-factor solution was therefore retained, in line with H1a. The results and factor loadings of the one-factor and the two-factor solutions are reported in Table 1.

As a robustness check, we ran the exploratory factor analyses a second time, treating the items as ordinals and using a robust diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) estimator with the weighted least squares means and variance-adjusted (WLSMV) parameter. The results were consistent with the maximum likelihood solution. Detailed results for this robustness check are available in Appendix 4.

Structure of the scale: Confirmatory factor analysis

As pre-registered, to further test the hypothesis that a two-factor model best fits the scale (H1a), a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted on the remaining sample of 1,845 participants using a robust maximum likelihood estimation.

The fit of the one-factor model was acceptable but below the prespecified thresholds (χ2 = 1,474(189), p < .001; RMSEA = .076 [.072; .080]; CFI = .914; TLI = .904; SRMR = .044). We evaluated the one-factor model further against dynamic fit index cutoffs. The onefactor model displayed a misfit that exceeded the most severe level of simulated cutoffs, which reinforces the conclusion drawn from the conventional cutoffs that a single factor does not adequately fit the data.

Model fit for the two-factor model approached but did not fully meet the prespecified cutoffs (χ2 = 986(188), p < .001; RMSEA = .060 [.056; .064]; CFI = .947; TLI = .940; SRMR = .036). The two-factor model was evaluated using the same dynamic fit index cutoffs and failed to reach the tailored cutoffs. The two latent factors were strongly correlated (r = .89 [.87; .91]), exceeding the correlation reported by Saks et al. (2015; r = .69). The item added by job counselors, related to sending unsolicited applications to get a job interview, loaded on the JSSE behavior subscale with standardized λ = .70 [.67; .73], indicating that the added item behaves consistently with the original scale.

As anticipated in our pre-registration and because the two-factor model did not fully meet the pre-specified fit criteria, we inspected the modification indices to locate the main source of local misfit. The largest one corresponded to a residual covariance between items "Get a job as soon as possible" and "Be invited for site visits." As both items refer to achieving concrete outcomes of the job search rather than enacting search behaviors, which plausibly produces shared variance beyond the common factor, we freely estimated this residual covariance. Adding this parameter improved the fit, with the scale meeting the prespecified cutoffs (χ² = 793(187), p < .001, RMSEA = .052 [.049,.056], CFI = .960, TLI = .955, SRMR = .033). For the rest of the article, the two-factor model refers to the model with no residual correlation.

The two-factor model was compared with the one-factor model. The two-factor solution fitted better (scaled chi-square difference test of Satorra-Bentler: Δχ 2 (1) = 265, p < .001), with lower information criteria (ΔAIC = 771; ΔBIC = 766) and improved fit across all indices (ΔRMSEA = .016; ΔCFI = .033; ΔTLI = .036; ΔSRMR = .008). Supporting H1a, the two-factor model was kept and is reported in Table 2.

As for exploratory factor analyses, robustness check treating the items as ordinals was again fitted. The ordinal solution reproduced both the two-factor structure and its high interfactor correlation. Detailed results for this robustness check are available in Appendix 4. Fit indices: χ2 = 986(188), p < .001; RMSEA = .060 [.056; .064]; CFI = .947; TLI = .940; SRMR = .036.

428

Structural validity: Measurement invariance 429

Not pre-registered, exploratory measurement invariance of the two-factor structure 430 was tested across both time points, age, gender, level of education, and length of registration 431 at the public employment service. Following Maassen et al. (2025), we conducted a series of 432 increasingly constrained multigroup CFA using a robust maximum likelihood estimator. We 433 tested configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance. The configural model estimated the 434 two-factor structure freely in each group and served as the baseline. The metric model 435 constrained factor loadings to be equal across groups. The scalar model constrained item 436 intercepts as well. The strict model constrained residual variances as well. 437

Overall, the scale demonstrated strict invariance across age, gender, level of education, 438 and length of registration, indicating that loadings, intercepts, and residual variances were 439 equivalent. It further demonstrated scalar invariance across time, with loadings and intercepts equivalent at T1 and T2 and only minor differences in residual variances. This finding supports the comparison of latent means, structural parameters, and observed composite scores across these groups, and interpreting the test-retest correlations as reflecting temporal stability of the construct rather than a change in its measurement. Full results are available in Appendix 5.

Internal consistency

The internal consistency of each scale was computed to test H1b. Internal consistency of the one-factor scale was ω = .95 [.94; .95] and α = .95 [.95; .95]. Internal consistency of the JSSE behavior subscale was ω = .90 [.89; .91] and α = .90 [.89; .91]. The alpha coefficient was close to the results reported by Saks et al. (2015), who found an alpha of .89. Internal consistency of the JSSE outcome subscale was ω = .93 [.93; .94] and α = .93 [0.93; 0.94].

Again, the alpha coefficient was close to the results of Saks et al. (2015), who reported an alpha of .96. The internal consistency indices supported H1b.

Test-retest reliability

Test-retest hypothesis H2 was assessed using Pearson correlations between T1 and T2, at a one-month interval (n = 859). Both JSSE behavior (r = .72 [.68, .75]) and outcome (r = .73 [.70, .76]) demonstrated strong stability over time. Hypothesis H2 was supported, as the confidence intervals of the scale and subscales did not include .60. A correlation matrix including JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome scores at both measurement time points is reported in Table 3.

Validity of the scale

Convergent validity

To test convergent validity hypotheses H3, H4a, and H4b, JSSE scores were correlated with self-esteem and with the autonomous motivation and amotivation subscales of the motivation to (re)work scale using Pearson correlations. Full correlations, including the motivation subscales for which no hypotheses were derived, are reported in Table 4. Supporting H3, both subscales were positively correlated with self-esteem (JSSE behavior: r = .39 [.35; .43]; JSSE outcome: r = .40 [.36; .43]). Although the confidence intervals did not include it, correlations were close to that reported by Creed et al. (2001; r = .50).

Consistent with H4a, both subscales were also positively correlated with autonomous motivation to (re)work (JSSE behavior: r = .31 [.27; .35]; JSSE outcome: r = .33 [.29; .36]).

The correlation observed for the total score was comparable to the correlation reported by Although not the focus of the hypotheses, the pattern of associations with the other motivation subscales also supported discriminant validity. The two subscales were essentially unrelated to identified regulation (JSSE behavior: r = .01 [-.04, .05]; JSSE outcome: r = -.01 [-.06, .03]) and were weakly negatively related to external social motivation (JSSE behavior: r = -.07 [-.11, -.02]; JSSE outcome: r = -.03 [-.08, .01]). A small positive association with external material motivation was observed (JSSE behavior: r = .17 [.12,.21]; JSSE outcome: r = .20 [.16,.24]).

Predictive validity: Estimation strategy

All models used JSSE subscales measured at T1 and included both JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome subscales. Because the two subscales are strongly correlated (r = .81 [.79; .82]), including them together means that each coefficient reflects the unique variance of one subscale while holding the other constant.

Therefore, coherent with Saks et al. (2015), coefficients should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than as the effect of each subscale.

Linear ordinary least squares regressions were used to examine the associations between JSSE and job search engagement. We report both unstandardized Β and standardized β coefficients. The standardized coefficients were obtained by standardizing both the predictor and the outcome, i.e., by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. They represent the expected change in the outcome in standard deviation units associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in the predictor.

Negative binomial count data regressions were used to predict, within 90 days, the number of applications a person sent to job postings, the time they spent on job boards, the number of clicks on job postings, the number of openings forwarded by a counselor, and the number of proposals sent by a recruiter (Venables & Ripley, 2002). Exponentiated coefficients are reported and represent incidence rate ratios (IRRs). An IRR above 1 indicates a higher expected count of outcomes for a one-unit increase in the predictor, and an IRR below 1 indicates a lower expected count of outcomes. Binary logistic regressions were used to predict, within 90 days, whether a person sent at least one application, spent at least one minute on the job board, clicked on at least one job offer, received at least one opening from a counselor, or received at least one proposal from a recruiter; and, within 150 days, whether the person found employment. Exponentiated coefficients are reported as odds ratios (ORs).

An OR above 1 indicates higher odds of the outcome, and an OR below 1 lower odds, for a one-unit increase in the predictor.

The same covariates as in Krug et al. (2019) were included in all models: gender, duration of unemployment, age, age squared, nationality, level of education, marital status, number of children to care for, administrative category, and type of support provided by the public employment service. The age-squared term was included to control for any nonlinear effects of age.

Predictive validity: Access to employment

To test H6 that only job search JSSE outcome would predict access to employment, we regressed whether the person obtained any kind of job, any standard employment, a permanent job, a fixed term job, and a temporary agency job, on job search behavior and JSSE outcome, including the covariates listed above. Results are reported in Table 6. Permanent job. JSSE behavior was associated with higher odds of obtaining a permanent job (OR = 1.49 [1.02; 2.16], SE = 0.28, z = 2.08, p = .037). JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining a permanent job (OR = 0.87 [0.64; 1.18], SE = 0.14, z = -0.89, p = .373). On the probability scale, an increase of one point in JSSE behavior increased the likelihood of obtaining a permanent job by 2.57 [0.15; 5] percentage points.

Fixed term job. JSSE behavior was not associated with obtaining a fixed-term job (OR = 1.01 [0.78; 1.29], SE = 0.13, z = 0.04, p = .967). Similarly, JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining a fixed-term job (OR = 0.98 [0.78; 1.22], SE = 0.11, z = -0.22, p = .828).

Temporary agency job. JSSE behavior was negatively associated with obtaining a temporary agency job (OR = 0.67 [0.49; 0.91], SE = 0.11, z = -2.54, p = .011). JSSE outcome was positively associated with obtaining a temporary agency job (OR = 1.44 [1.08; 1.92], SE = 0.21, z = 2.51, p = .012). Robustness check

As shown in Appendix 2, respondents differed from non-respondents on nearly all measured sociodemographics. To check that this did not bias our results, we re-estimated all predictive models using inverse-probability weighting, which weights respondents by the inverse of their estimated probability of responding. The predictors of responding to the survey were selected by LASSO regression. Full results are reported in Appendix 6.

The signs and magnitudes were comparable to those of the main analyses across all outcomes and predictors. JSSE behavior remained positively associated with the number of applications sent, the probability of sending at least one application, and job search engagement. JSSE outcome remained negatively associated with behavioral outcomes. The associations with access to employment were also unchanged, with JSSE behavior predicting permanent employment, and JSSE outcome predicting temporary agency work. Since these weights correct for observed differences between respondents and non-respondents, the stability of the results suggests that observed selection does not drive our conclusions.

However, selection based on unobserved characteristics, such as non-respondents' selfesteem, cannot be ruled out as these weights only correct for the observed covariates included in the model.

Discussion

This study translated and validated a French version of the job search self-efficacy (JSSE) scale developed by Saks et al. (2015) among a large sample of unemployed people, assessing its structure, reliability, convergent and predictive validity.

Structure and reliability of the scale

Consistent with H1a, both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses showed that a two-factor solution reproduced the theoretical distinction between JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome, and fitted better than a one-factor solution. These results were replicated when accounting for the ordinal nature of the items. The correlations between the two latent factors, as well as between the two observed factors, were stronger than reported by Saks et al. (2015).

Exploratory measurement invariance testing showed that strict invariance held across age, gender, level of education and length of registration, while scalar invariance was found across a one-month interval. The two-factor confirmatory model did not meet the more stringent dynamic fit index cutoffs (McNeish & Wolf, 2023). Consistent with H1b, both subscales showed strong reliability, with omegas and alphas above .90, in line with Saks et al. (2015). Supporting H2, the test-retest reliability of the scale over a one-month interval was excellent, with Pearson correlations above r = .72 and confidence intervals excluding .60. Considered jointly, these results indicate a two-factor scale that is coherent with the theoretical distinction between JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome, although latent factors were strongly correlated.

Validity of the scale

Supporting H3, H4a and H4b, both subscales correlated in the expected direction with self-esteem, autonomous motivation to (re)work, and amotivation to (re)work, respectively.

Contrary to expectation, the correlations with self-esteem were not equivalent to that reported by Creed et al. (2001; r = .50), but were close. Contrary to our expectation, correlations with autonomous motivation and amotivation were not stronger than those reported by Camus et al. (2017), the former being equivalent and the latter slightly weaker. Exploratory analyses further showed that both subscales were essentially unrelated to identified regulation, very weakly and negatively related to external social motivation, and weakly and positively related to external material motivation.

These associations position JSSE along the self-determination continuum, correlating most strongly with autonomous motivation and negatively with amotivation. This supports the idea that JSSE is a domain-specific evaluation of one's abilities rather than a general motivation proxy or a general self-evaluation. In sum, these results place JSSE as a proximal but distinct concept from motivation and self-esteem.

Predictive validity of the scale

Consistent with H5a, JSSE behavior positively predicted the number of applications sent, the probability of sending at least one application, and overall job search engagement. However, it was not a predictor of platform browsing behavior, such as the time spent viewing job ads, the number of clicks on job offers, or the probability of engaging in these activities. Nevertheless, all of these coefficients pointed in the expected positive direction, and several approached significance. Thus, H5a was only partially supported. Theoretically, JSSE behavior is related to action and concrete goal setting (Lent & Brown, 2013; van Hooft et al., 2021) and targets "specific job search behaviors" (Saks et al., 2015, p. 105). Our results are consistent with this definition, as sending an application is a discrete, self-initiated act with the clear objective to obtain an interview and, ultimately, a job. In contrast, browsing or clicking on job ads is diffuse and only serves the intermediate goal of finding opportunities.

Its payoff largely lies outside the individual's control since time spent searching may or may not yield results. Thus, our overall pattern of results supports the idea that JSSE behavior relates to specific, targeted job search activities, such as sending applications, rather than to more general activities, such as browsing employment platforms. This aligns with Kim et al.'s (2019, p. 28) conclusion that JSSE behaviors "have a more meaningful relationship with the activities and resources used for job searching than with the actual time spent in the job search." Contrary to H5b, JSSE outcome negatively predicted all of these behaviors. Since the two subscales were highly correlated, including them in the same model means that each coefficient reflects only the unique variance of one subscale when the other is held constant. This should not be interpreted as evidence that expecting favorable outcomes reduces job searching, but suggests that, among individuals with the same level of JSSE behavior, those with higher JSSE outcome search less. H5c assumed two positive effects, with a stronger coefficient for JSSE behavior than for JSSE outcome, and is not supported on either count.

First, the two subscales predicted job search behavior in opposite rather than similar directions. Second, the absolute effects did not differ in magnitude across all outcomes.

Contrary to H6, JSSE behavior predicted a higher likelihood of obtaining a permanent job, and a lower likelihood of obtaining a temporary agency job. Moreover, also contrary to H6, JSSE outcome only predicted access to a temporary agency job. Therefore, when job search effort is held constant, individuals who are more confident in their ability to obtain employment are more likely to enter temporary agency work. In contrast, individuals who are more confident in their ability to conduct the job search itself are less likely to do so and more likely to obtain a permanent job. One interpretation is that JSSE outcome captures confidence in obtaining any kind of employment, regardless of its quality or stability. Under this reading, unemployed people high in JSSE outcome would be more available for readily accessible positions, of which temporary agency work is the most immediate and least selective. JSSE behavior, on the other hand, could support a sustained and targeted job search and could therefore orient unemployed people toward permanent employment. However, this interpretation should be taken with caution as it is post hoc. Overall, contrary to H6, access to employment was largely unrelated to JSSE. This finding is consistent with the idea that selfefficacy is a proximal determinant of job search behavior, but a distal predictor of employment, which depends heavily on labor market conditions and employer decisions that lie beyond the individual (Kanfer et al., 2001; Lent & Brown, 2013).

Exploratory research questions

In response to RQ1 and RQ2, neither JSSE behavior nor JSSE outcome predicted the number of job openings forwarded by a counselor, the number of job proposals initiated by a recruiter, nor the probability of receiving at least one of these. Therefore, these two channels to employment were unrelated to JSSE, complementing the results of H6. Considered as a whole, the convergence across the three channels reinforces the idea that self-efficacy is a proximal determinant of job search behavior for unemployed people, but a distal predictor of employment that lies beyond one's behavior, as well as the judgments and decisions of counselors and recruiters.

Finally, addressing RQ3, JSSE behavior and outcome varied according to several sociodemographic characteristics. Since all predictors were included in the models, these are partial associations adjusted for the remaining covariates. Specifically, men, non-French participants, and participants with dependent children reported higher self-efficacy, primarily on JSSE outcome. In contrast, participants with no diploma reported lower JSSE behavior, and those seeking part-time open-ended contracts reported lower self-efficacy on both subscales. We had no specific hypotheses about these associations and present them as exploratory findings. The clearest pattern was related to the intensity of support provided by the employment service. Unemployed people who received guided, reinforced, or very reinforced support reported progressively lower JSSE behavior and outcome than those who received regular follow-up. The fact that the scale tracks this is a favorable sign for its validity and supports its use in identifying unemployed people who may benefit the most from targeted intervention.

These results support the validity of the French translation of the JSSE scale, at least among unemployed people in France. This conclusion is supported by several strengths that address limitations of prior research, including a large sample size of 2,055 unemployed people, objective indicators of job search behavior and access to employment drawn from administrative records, a longitudinal design spanning 90-and 150-day windows, and the ruling out of a measurement effect (Saks et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2025).

The signs and magnitudes were comparable across all outcomes and predictors, indicating that the observed selection does not drive our conclusions.

Conclusion

In this study, we thoroughly translated and validated the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale among unemployed people in France. The French version reproduced the original's two-factor structure, demonstrated high reliability, remained stable over one month, and was largely invariant across age, gender, education level, unemployment duration, and across a one-month interval. This makes the French version suitable for research and applied use, as well as for comparing groups of unemployed people. Furthermore, job search self-efficacy behavior positively predicted the number of job applications sent within 90 days, while job search self-efficacy outcome negatively predicted it. Finally, job search self-efficacy behavior positively predicted access to a permanent job and negatively predicted access to a temporary agency job, while job search self-efficacy outcome only predicted access to a temporary agency job. However, the two subscales were very strongly correlated in this population, and their distinct predictive value should be better established.

Overall, the French JSSE scale is a psychometrically sound measure that can support future research and interventions on job searching in French-speaking settings.

Implications for research and practice

JSSE has been measured in multiple, and sometimes non-comparable, ways in past literature (Saks et al., 2015). By translating a validated and coherent scale into French, we provide French-speaking scholars with a measure that distinguishes JSSE behavior from JSSE outcome, which is valuable in multiple theoretical frameworks that include self-efficacy as a component of models aiming to explore the job search process. Further validation beyond the French unemployment context is pending.

The scale could also benefit applied settings, as its temporal stability makes it suitable for evaluating the effectiveness of interventions in improving JSSE (Eden & Aviram, 1993; Liu et al., 2014; Price et al., 1992; Roques, 2008; Van Ryn & Vinokur, 1992; Vinokur & Schul, 1997). Additionally, its ability to identify unemployed people most in need of support, as demonstrated by its correlation with the level of support provided by the employment service, is valuable for pinpointing unemployed people who require additional assistance (van Hooft et al., 2021; Wanberg et al., 2010). Future research could define thresholds that would help both researchers and practitioners in identifying unemployed people in need of specific help with their job search.

Limitations

The first limitation is that, in this sample, the two subscales were highly correlated at the observed level, and very highly at the latent level. While remaining structurally distinct and invariant, the two subscales shared much of their variance and largely measured the same construct. On a positive note, the regression models did not show elevated variance inflation factors. Future studies could use cognitive interviewing to determine if respondents can distinguish between the two sets of items and examine if the subscales provide distinct predictive information in samples where the two beliefs are less correlated. In addition to the strong covariance between the subscales, the internal consistency within each subscale is high. The alphas and omegas for the JSSE behavior subscale reach the threshold of .90, while the alphas and omegas for the JSSE outcome subscale exceed it. While this result aligns with that of Saks et al. (2015), it also suggests that some items are redundant. Future research could focus on creating a shorter version of the scale to reduce redundancy and improve usability.

Second, job search behavior and access to employment were obtained from the information system of the French public employment service. While this yields objective and unobtrusive measures, it only captures job search activity recorded on the public platform.

Although the database contains over one million job openings and is a valuable resource, participants may have used it infrequently, browsed without logging in, or relied on other job boards whose usage records we could not access. Thus, part of their true job search effort went unobserved, which may weaken the associations with self-efficacy. Nevertheless, we consider the administrative measure a strength because Marinescu and Skandalis (2021) have demonstrated that the database and its online applications reliably capture the overall job search process. Another limitation is that our job search behavior and job search outcome measures differed from those of Saks et al. (2015), who used self-reported job search behavior and the number of job offers received. This prevented a direct comparison with their predictive results. That said, Saks et al. (2015) surveyed self-reported intentions and behavior over a two-month period. In contrast, our administrative outcomes objectively recorded actual behavior and employment status within three and five months respectively. Thus, the two approaches provide complementary evidence from different measurement perspectives.

Third, the response rate was low, and respondents differed markedly from nonrespondents on nearly all observed characteristics (Appendix 2), consistent with an overrepresentation of more engaged unemployed people. To address this selection, robustness analyses reweighting the sample by the inverse probability of responding were conducted.

H5a) and JSSE outcome (H5b) would predict job search behavior, with the former showing a larger effect than the latter (H5c). Furthermore, we only expected JSSE outcome to predict access to employment (H6; van Hooft et al., 2021). We could not directly compare the results of the JSSE behavior subscale with those of Saks et al. (2015) because they used a 10-item self-report scale to measure job search behavior, whereas we counted the number of applications sent. Similarly, we could not directly compare the results of the JSSE outcome subscale with those of Saks et al. (2015) because they measured job search outcomes as the number of job offers received, whereas we measured it by determining whether the person had found employment.

To test whether JSSE behavior (H5a) and JSSE outcome (H5b) would predict job search behavior, we regressed the number of applications sent within 90 days, whether the person sent at least one application within 90 days, the time spent looking at job ads within 90 days, whether the person spent any time looking at job ads within 90 days, the number of clicks on job offers within 90 days, whether the person clicked on at least one ad on the job search platform, and a general job search engagement, on JSSE behavior, JSSE outcome, with covariates listed above. To test whether JSSE behavior would have a stronger effect than JSSE outcome (H5c), the average marginal effects on the response scale were compared, using "HC3" robust standard errors (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024). Results are reported in Table5. Number of applications sent within 90 days. JSSE behavior was associated with a higher application count (IRR = 1.40 [1.07; 1.83], SE = 0.19, z = 2.44, p = .015), while JSSE outcome was associated with a lower count (IRR = 0.69 [0.54; 0.88], SE = 0.08, z = -3.03, p = .002). On the response scale, this represents 0.17 [0.03; 0.31] more applications for a onepoint increase in JSSE behavior, and -0.19 [-0.31; -0.06] for a one-point increase in JSSE outcome. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly smaller than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.02 [-0.10; 0.07], p = .678). Sending at least one application within 90 days. JSSE behavior was associated with higher odds of sending at least one application (OR = 1.35 [1.05; 1.75], SE = 0.18, z = 2.32, p = .021), while JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.75 [0.60; 0.94], SE = 0.08, z = -2.55, p = .011). On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE behavior raised the likelihood of sending an application by 3.58 [0.55; 6.60] percentage points. Conversely, an increase of one point in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood by -3.42 [6.04; -0.80] percentage points. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly larger than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = 0.16 [-1.61; 1.92], p = .861). Time spent looking at job ads within 90 days. JSSE behavior was not associated with time spent (IRR = 1.31 [0.95; 1.81], SE = 0.22, z = 1.62, p = .105), but JSSE outcome was associated with spending less time (IRR = 0.74 [0.56; 0.97], SE = 0.10, z = -2.18, p = .030). On the response scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome corresponded to -1.54 [-2.97; -0.12] minutes spent on the platform. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.19 [-1.18; 0.80], p = .705). Spending any time looking at job ads within 90 days. JSSE behavior was not associated with spending time on job ads (OR = 1.24 [0.97; 1.59], SE = 0.15, z = 1.75, p = .081), whereas JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.78 [0.63; 0.97], SE = 0.09, z = -2.19, p = .029). On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood of spending time on job ads by -2.99 [-5.66; -0.31] percentage points. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly smaller than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.31 [-2.14; 1.51], p = .737). Number of clicks on job offers within 90 days. JSSE behavior was not associated with the number of clicks (IRR = 1.30 [0.99; 1.70], SE = 0.18, z = 1.88, p = .060). However, JSSE outcome was associated with fewer clicks (IRR = 0.72 [0.57; 0.92], SE = 0.09, z = -2.69, p = .007). On the response scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome corresponded to approximately -0.37 [-0.65; -0.09] clicks. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.08 [-0.27; 0.12], p = .434). At least one click on the job search platform. JSSE behavior was not associated with clicking on job offers (OR = 1.23 [0.98; 1.53], SE = 0.14, z = 1.77, p = .076). JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.81 [0.66; 0.99], SE = 0.08, z = -2.09, p = .037). On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood of clicking on a job offer by -3.04 [-5.90; -0.19] percentage points. The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.15 [-2.08; 1.77], p = .877).

Any kind of job (permanent, fixed term, or temporary agency employment). JSSE behavior was not associated with obtaining any job (OR = 0.93 [0.76; 1.14], SE = 0.10, z = -0.67, p = .506). Similarly, JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining any job (OR = 1.09 [0.91; 1.30], SE = 0.10, z = 0.96, p = .338). Any standard employment (permanent or fixed term employment). JSSE behavior was not associated with obtaining standard employment (OR = 1.13 [0.91; 1.40], SE = 0.12, z = 1.10, p = .271). Similarly, JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining standard employment (OR = 0.97 [0.81; 1.17], SE = 0.09, z = -0.29, p = .769).

Nationality. Compared with French participants, non-French participants reported higher JSSE outcome (Β = 0.19 [0.04; 0.35], SE = 0.08, t = 2.40, p = .017; β = 0.19 [0.04; 0.35]). Participants with two children also reported higher JSSE outcome (Β = 0.16 [0.03; 0.29], SE = 0.07, t = 2.47, p = .014); β = 0.16 [0.03; 0.29]), with no difference in JSSE behavior.

Neither JSSE behavior nor JSSE outcome predicted the number of proposals a recruiter sent within 90 days. JSSE behavior was not associated with the number of proposals (IRR = 0.99 [0.72; 1.36], SE = 0.16, z = -0.05, p = .962), nor was JSSE outcome (IRR = 1.02 [0.76; 1.36], SE = 0.15, z = 0.14, p = .890). Likewise, neither subscale predicted whether the person received at least one proposal (JSSE behavior: OR = 1.07 [0.79; 1.47], SE = 0.17, z = 0.45, p = .654; JSSE outcome: OR = 0.90 [0.68; 1.19], SE = 0.13, z = -0.74, p = .461).

Gender.

Compared with women, men reported higher JSSE outcome (Β = 0.15 [0.05; 0.24], SE = 0.05, t = 3.13, p = .002; β = 0.15 [0.05; 0.24]). Gender was not associated with JSSE behavior.Level of education.Compared with participants with an A-level education, participants with below A-level education with no diploma reported lower JSSE behavior (Β = -0.25 [-0.44; -0.06], SE = 0.10, t = -2.59, p = .010; β = -0.28 [-0.49; -0.07]), and participants with at least two years of higher education reported lower JSSE outcome (Β = -0.15 [-0.28; -0.03], SE = 0.06, t = -2.44, p = .015; β = -0.15 [-0.28; -0.03]). Administrative category. Compared with participants in administrative category 1 (unemployed, available to work, required to search for a full-time open-ended contract), participants in administrative category 2 (unemployed, available to work, required to search for a part-time open-ended contract) reported lower JSSE behavior (Β = -0.20 [-0.32; -0.07], SE = 0.06, t = -3.04, p = .002; β = -0.22 [-0.37; -0.08]) and JSSE outcome (Β = -0.20 [-0.35; -0.06], SE = 0.07, t = -2.81, p = .005; β = -0.20 [-0.35; -0.06]).
